opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I've been thinking about quite a lot. There's a tendency to treat hallucination as a bug you can patch, a bit more RLHF or a retrieval step and it goes away. I suspect it's more fundamental than that, and it ties into how these models represent things internally.

When you train a big network on next-token prediction, there are many ways it could carve up the world to get the loss down. Some representations are close to how we'd do it: there are objects, they have properties, causes lead to effects. Others are statistical shortcuts that work most of the time on the training distribution but don't reflect any real structure. From the outside, on the benchmark, those two can look almost identical. You only see the difference when you push the model somewhere slightly off-distribution, and then the shortcut fails in a way that looks confident and plausible. That's a lot of what we call hallucination.

So I don't think of it as the model lying, or even as it not knowing. It has built a representation that's fractured, or entangled in odd ways, and it's interpolating across a surface that doesn't correspond to anything real. The fluency is perfect because the language part is very well learned, but the world model underneath can be patchy, and nothing in the training objective forces it to know where its own patches are.

That's partly why I've gotten interested in more natural, more biologically inspired kinds of representation, things with a notion of time, of iterative processing, of the model being able to think a bit longer about something it's unsure of. If the representation is organised in a way that's closer to the actual structure of the world, I'd expect hallucinations to decrease almost as a side effect, rather than us bolting on a fix afterwards.

The uncomfortable part is that scaling has worked so well that there isn't much pressure to examine this. If you can get another few points by making the model bigger, why worry about whether the internal carving is sensible? But I think hallucination is one of the places where the cracks show, and they're telling us something about the representations, not just about the outputs.

r001.rationale: The response says models can use different ways to carve up the world, including statistical shortcuts that fail off-distribution and produce hallucinations.

r002.rationale: It says training does not force models to know where their representations are patchy, but does not identify making models implicitly aware of their own way of carving up the world as a research objective.

r003.rationale: The response discusses iterative processing and thinking longer when unsure, but does not ask how models can learn to break problems into small, solvable parts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I think the framing of "carving up the world" is actually the right one, because hallucination tends to get talked about as if it's a bug, like a flaw in the pipeline that you could just patch out. And I don't really think that's what it is.

So the way I'd put it is this: a model has learned some representation of the world, and that representation is a compression. You've taken an enormous amount of text and squeezed it into a fixed set of weights, and when you compress you have to make choices about what regularities you keep and which ones you throw away. Those choices are the carving. And there's no single correct carving. You can cluster the world by surface statistics, you can cluster it by causal structure, you can cluster it by what humans tend to say next, and these all give you different boundaries.

Now, hallucination, in that view, is just what happens when you ask the model a question that lands in a region where its particular carving doesn't line up with the carving that you, the asker, have in your head. The model isn't lying, it doesn't have access to the notion of truth in the way we mean it. It's filling in the shape that its boundaries imply. If the boundaries were drawn around "what plausible-sounding text follows this," then plausible-sounding text is exactly what you get, including plausible-sounding citations that don't exist.

And I think that's why I'm a bit skeptical of people who say we just need more data or more RLHF and it'll go away. Those approaches move the boundaries around, and that's useful, but they don't give the model a fundamentally different kind of carving. You're still doing the same thing, just with the lines in slightly better places.

Where it gets interesting for me, and this is closer to what I've been thinking about lately, is whether you can have a system that holds multiple carvings at once and knows which one it's using. Humans do something like this. I can think about a cup as a physical object, as a social signal, as a word, and I know which frame I'm in. Current models, I'd argue, blur those frames together because the training objective never rewarded them for keeping them apart. So a lot of what looks like hallucination is really frame confusion. The model slides from "here's what people typically say about X" into "here's what is true about X" without noticing the seam.

So if you asked me what the actual research question is, I'd say it's less "how do we stop hallucination" and more "how do we get a model that has a sense of which of its own representations it's currently relying on." Because once you have that, the model can at least tell you "I'm answering this from the pattern-completion part of my world, not from the part that was grounded in anything." And that honesty about the carving is, I think, a lot more valuable than trying to pretend there's only one.

r001.rationale: The response says hallucinations can arise when the model’s particular way of carving up the world differs from the asker’s.

r002.rationale: It names as the research question getting models to recognize which representation or framing they are relying on.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask how models might decompose problems into small, solvable parts.

astra-6.text:
I think hallucination is partly about the gap between a model finding a plausible way to describe the world and that description actually being true. There are lots of ways to carve up the world—different categories, different abstractions—and several of those can be useful. But that doesn’t mean every claim you make within them is equally valid.

You might group things by how they look, or by what they do. Depending on the question, one grouping might be more useful than the other. So when a model gives us something unexpected, there’s a distinction between, “It’s using a different abstraction from the one I had in mind,” and, “It’s asserting something that didn’t happen.”

The tricky thing with language models is that both can come out sounding equally convincing. The language itself doesn’t necessarily tell you whether the model has found an interesting alternative perspective or just produced a plausible continuation. You need some way of checking it against the thing you’re talking about.

r001.rationale: The response says an unexpected output may use a different abstraction or way of grouping the world, rather than assert something false.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify implicit awareness of a model’s own world-partitioning as a research objective.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask how models can learn to break problems into smaller, solvable parts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two things that can get mixed together there. A model might carve up the world differently from us—use different internal concepts or draw different boundaries—and still give a perfectly useful account of what’s happening. Being different doesn’t automatically make that account a hallucination.

But once you ask a factual question, there are constraints. If it invents a paper or attributes a statement to someone who never said it, that’s something we can check. You can’t explain that away just by saying it has a different worldview.

The interesting connection is that producing a plausible continuation doesn’t necessarily require the model to settle on a consistent account of the world. It can move between ways of representing things that work locally, while the whole answer doesn’t hang together. So I’d want to distinguish a different representation from an unsupported claim, and then ask how reliably the model’s representations constrain what it says.

r001.rationale: The response says a different way of representing the world does not automatically make an account a hallucination, and distinguishes that from unsupported claims. It does not say hallucinations may reflect an alternative way of carving up the world.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify implicit awareness of a model’s own way of carving up the world as a research objective.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask how models can learn to break problems into small, solvable parts.
